_note: Name-facts for Russia (FT-41, docs/PLAN_V0.9.md). See italy.json for
Russia's regions come in two kinds and it is worth knowing which you
are looking at. The oblasts and krais are almost all named after their
main city, which is in turn named after its river - Tomsk on the Tom,
Omsk on the Om, Kursk on the Kur. The republics are named after a
PEOPLE, and those names are the interesting half of the map: Tatars,
Bashkirs, Chuvash, Mari, Komi, Buryats, Tuvans, Sakha, Chechens.
Useful endings:  -sk = a place (usually on the named river)
The map uses Natural Earth's labels, so some are the short form
(Moskva and Moskovskaya are the city and the oblast around it) and a
few use older or transliterated spellings - Chita for Zabaykalsky,
Yevrey for the Jewish Autonomous Oblast.
arkhangelsk: "Archangel" — named for a monastery of the Archangel Michael at the mouth of the Northern Dvina.
It was Russia's only sea port for over a century, until Peter the Great built St Petersburg.
Allied Arctic convoys delivered supplies here in the Second World War, through ice and U-boats.
nenets: Named for the Nenets people, whose own name means simply "man" — as many indigenous names do.
They still herd reindeer across the tundra in the largest surviving nomadic pastoral system in the Arctic.
It has one of the smallest populations of any Russian region, about 42,000 people in an area the size of England and Scotland.
murmansk: From an old Russian name for the Norwegians, murman, a corruption of "Norman".
The largest city north of the Arctic Circle anywhere in the world, and its port never freezes because of the Gulf Stream.
The Kola superdeep borehole here reached 12,262 m, the deepest hole ever drilled, and found water where none was expected.
yamal-nenets: Yamal means "the end of the earth" in Nenets, and the peninsula is exactly that.
It produces most of Russia's natural gas — a large share of the world's proven reserves lies under it.
Thawing permafrost here has opened craters by explosive methane release and, in 2016, released anthrax from a thawed reindeer carcass.
chukotka: Named for the Chukchi, whose name for themselves means "rich in reindeer".
Only 82 km from Alaska across the strait, and the two Diomede Islands in it are split by the date line — one is tomorrow.
The easternmost region, where Russia's day begins, and one of the coldest inhabited places on earth.
krasnoyarsk: "Red ravine" — krasny red, yar a steep bank: the fort was built on a red clay bluff in 1628.
The second largest region in Russia, running 3,000 km from the Arctic to Mongolia.
Norilsk in it is one of the most polluted places in the world from nickel smelting, and one of the northernmost cities anywhere.
sakha-yakutia: Sakha is the people's own name; Yakut is what the Russians called them, borrowed from a neighbouring language.
The largest subnational entity in the world, about the size of India, with under a million people.
Oymyakon in it is the coldest permanently inhabited place on earth, at −67.7 °C, and it produces most of Russia's diamonds.
komi: Named for the Komi people, whose language is Finno-Ugric and related to Finnish and Hungarian.
Its virgin Komi forests are the largest untouched boreal forest in Europe and a UNESCO site.
Vorkuta in it was one of the largest Gulag camps; the city was built by prisoners to mine coal in the Arctic.
karelia: Named for the Karelians, a Finnic people; the name may come from a word for a herd or for highland.
Most of it was Finnish until 1940, and about 400,000 Finns left rather than live under Soviet rule.
Kizhi on Lake Onega has a wooden church of twenty-two domes built in 1714 without a single nail, a UNESCO site.
magadan: Probably from Even monghodan, "sea dwellings", or a similar coastal word.
It was the gateway to the Kolyma Gulag: hundreds of thousands passed through its port to the gold mines, and many did not return.
The Road of Bones inland was built by and over prisoners, and is still the only land route.
khanty-mansiy: Named for two related Finno-Ugric peoples, the Khanty and the Mansi.
It produces about half of Russia's oil, from the West Siberian basin.
Its indigenous peoples number only a few tens of thousands among 1.7 million incomers drawn by that oil.
vologda: From a Finno-Ugric root meaning "white" or "clear", the name of the river.
Its butter, made with a distinctive nutty flavour from a nineteenth-century method, is a protected Russian name.
Ivan the Terrible considered making it his capital and built a kremlin there before changing his mind.
city-of-st-petersburg: Named by Peter the Great for his patron saint, not for himself — and in Dutch-German form, Sankt Piterburkh, because he admired the Dutch.
Built on marsh from 1703 at enormous cost in lives, and the capital for two centuries.
It was besieged for 872 days in the Second World War as Leningrad; about a million civilians died, mostly of starvation.
leningrad: The oblast around St Petersburg, which kept the Soviet name when the city changed back in 1991.
Staraya Ladoga in it was possibly the first capital of Rus, founded by Scandinavians in the 750s.
The Road of Life across frozen Lake Ladoga here was the only supply route into the besieged city.
sverdlovsk: Named for Yakov Sverdlov, a Bolshevik organiser; the city reverted to Yekaterinburg in 1991 but the oblast did not.
Yekaterinburg is where the last tsar and his family were shot in 1918, and a cathedral now stands on the site.
The Urals here are the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia, marked by an obelisk on the road out of the city.
perm: From a Finno-Ugric phrase, probably perä maa, "the far land", which the Russians took as the region's name.
The Permian geological period is named after it — the last period before the dinosaurs, defined from rocks here in 1841.
Kungur ice cave in the region has grottoes that stay frozen year-round.
kirov: Named for Sergei Kirov, the party boss whose 1934 assassination Stalin used as the pretext for the Great Purge.
The city was Vyatka before that, after its river, and there is a long-running campaign to change it back.
Dymkovo toys, brightly painted clay figures made here since the 1400s, are a Russian folk-art standard.
kostroma: Named for the river, itself possibly from a Slavic figure of the same name burned in effigy at midsummer.
The Romanov dynasty began here: the Ipatiev monastery is where Mikhail Romanov was offered the throne in 1613.
It is part of the Golden Ring of old Russian towns, and its centre was rebuilt on a fan-shaped plan after a fire.
tomsk: Named for the Tom river, from a Ket or Turkic word for a river.
The first university in Siberia opened here in 1888, and it is still the most student-dense city in Russia.
Its wooden lace architecture — carved window surrounds on timber houses — is the best preserved in the country.
novgorod: "New town" — and it is one of the oldest in Russia, first mentioned in 859.
Veliky Novgorod was a merchant republic for three centuries, with an assembly that hired and fired its princes, until Moscow crushed it in 1478.
Birchbark letters dug up here, over a thousand of them, show that ordinary townspeople — including women and children — could read and write.
kamchatka: Probably from a river name, or from the Itelmen word for a local people.
It has about 300 volcanoes, 29 of them active, and they are a UNESCO site.
Closed to outsiders, even Soviet citizens, until 1990, and its Valley of the Geysers was only found in 1941.
yaroslavl: Named for Yaroslav the Wise, who founded it around 1010 — legend says on the spot where he killed a bear with an axe, which is on the city's arms.
Its centre is a UNESCO site, laid out on a radial plan by Catherine the Great.
Russia's first professional theatre opened here in 1750.
irkutsk: Named for the Irkut river, from a Buryat word.
Lake Baikal is here: the deepest lake in the world at 1,642 m, holding about a fifth of all unfrozen fresh water on earth.
Exiled Decembrist officers settled in the city after 1825 and turned a frontier town into "the Paris of Siberia".
tyumen: Probably from a Turkic phrase meaning "ten thousand", the size of a Tatar military unit.
The first Russian town in Siberia, founded in 1586 on the site of a Tatar khanate capital.
The oil and gas of the West Siberian basin is administered from here, which makes it one of Russia's richest regions.
pskov: From the river Pskova, probably from a Baltic or Finnic root meaning "pitch" or "resin".
Another medieval merchant republic, with its own law code, absorbed by Moscow in 1510.
Pushkin is buried at Svyatogorsky monastery here, near the estate where he was exiled and wrote much of Eugene Onegin.
tver: From a Finnic river name, Tikhvera; it was Kalinin in Soviet times and changed back in 1990.
Tver was Moscow's main rival for leadership of the Russian lands in the 1300s and lost.
Afanasy Nikitin, a merchant from here, reached India in the 1460s — thirty years before Vasco da Gama — and wrote it up.
udmurt: Named for the Udmurt people; the name may combine a word for meadow with murt, "man".
Izhevsk in it is where Kalashnikov designed and built the AK-47, and the factory still makes them.
Udmurt is a Finno-Ugric language, and the region has one of the highest shares of red-haired people in the world.
ivanovo: From the personal name Ivan — the town grew from a village called Ivanovo.
It was the centre of Russian textiles and is still called the city of brides, because the mills employed mostly women.
The first workers' soviet in Russian history was formed here in 1905, two years before the better-known ones.
mariy-el: "Mari land" — el means land in Mari, so the name is the people plus their country.
The Mari kept their own pagan religion later than almost anyone in Europe, and sacred groves are still used for ceremonies.
Mari is Finno-Ugric, and the republic is one of the most forested in European Russia.
nizhegorod: From Nizhny Novgorod, "the lower new town" — lower than Novgorod, and downstream.
It stands where the Oka meets the Volga, and its trade fair was the largest in the Russian Empire.
Closed to foreigners in Soviet times, which is why Sakharov was exiled here; it was called Gorky then.
omsk: Named for the Om river, from a Baraba Tatar word meaning "quiet".
It was the capital of White Russia under Admiral Kolchak in 1918–19, and the imperial gold reserve was held here.
Dostoevsky served four years at hard labour in its prison, which became The House of the Dead.
vladimir: Named for Vladimir Monomakh or Vladimir the Great — the name itself means "ruler of the world" or "famous for power".
It was the capital of Rus before Moscow, and its white stone churches are a UNESCO site.
The Vladimirka road east from here was the route convicts walked to Siberia, and the name became a byword for exile.
moskovskaya: The oblast around Moscow, taking the city's name; the city itself is a separate region on this map.
Sergiev Posad in it holds the Trinity Lavra, the spiritual centre of the Russian Orthodox Church.
Star City here trained every Soviet and Russian cosmonaut, and still trains those who fly to the space station.
kurgan: Russian for a burial mound — the Scythian and later kurgans scattered across its steppe.
Gavriil Ilizarov developed his bone-lengthening frame here in the 1950s, and patients came from around the world to a provincial Siberian town.
It is one of the main grain-growing regions of the trans-Ural steppe.
chuvash: Named for the Chuvash, whose language is the only surviving member of the Oghur branch of Turkic — quite unlike Tatar or Turkish.
They are probably descended from the Volga Bulgars, whose other branch ended up in the Balkans as Bulgarians.
It is the most densely populated republic in the Volga region and grows most of Russia's hops.
moskva: The city itself, named for the river; the river's name is probably Finno-Ugric or Baltic, perhaps meaning wet or marshy.
It has been the capital since 1480, except for the two centuries when St Petersburg was.
Its metro stations were built as "palaces for the people", with chandeliers and mosaics, and some are 84 m underground.
tatarstan: Named for the Tatars, whose name the Mongols' European enemies confused with Tartarus, the classical hell — which is why old maps say Tartary.
Kazan, its capital, was the seat of a khanate until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1552; its kremlin is a UNESCO site.
About half the population is Muslim Tatar and half Orthodox Russian, and both languages are official.
novosibirsk: "New Siberian town" — founded in 1893 where the Trans-Siberian Railway crossed the Ob.
It reached a million people faster than any city in history at the time, in under seventy years.
Akademgorodok outside it was built in 1957 as a science city in the forest, and still holds dozens of research institutes.
kaliningrad: Named for Mikhail Kalinin, a Soviet figurehead — it was Königsberg, "king's mountain", founded by the Teutonic Knights in 1255.
An exclave: it borders Poland and Lithuania and has no land connection to the rest of Russia.
Kant was born, taught and died here and never left the city; his tomb is on the cathedral wall.
smolensk: Probably from smola, "pitch" or "tar", which was made here for caulking boats on the Dnieper route.
It has been the western gate to Moscow for a thousand years, and Napoleon and Hitler both fought major battles for it.
Its city wall of 1602, 6.5 km with 38 towers, was called the necklace of Russia.
khabarovsk: Named for Yerofey Khabarov, a seventeenth-century explorer whose treatment of the Amur peoples was brutal enough that Moscow recalled him.
The city sits on the Amur, directly across from China, and the river freezes solid enough to drive on.
The region is the size of Germany and Poland together, with 1.3 million people.
kemerovo: From a family name or from kemer, a Turkic word for a riverbank.
The Kuzbass coalfield here produces most of Russia's coal.
Tomskaya Pisanitsa in it has rock carvings up to 4,000 years old on cliffs above the Tom.
mordovia: Named for the Mordvins, two Finno-Ugric peoples — the Erzya and the Moksha — whose languages are not mutually intelligible.
The republic hosted World Cup matches in 2018 in a stadium built for a city of 300,000.
It has long held a large share of Russia's prison camps, a legacy of the Gulag-era Dubravlag system.
ryazan: Possibly from a word for a cut or a slope, or from the Erzya people.
Old Ryazan was destroyed by the Mongols in 1237 and never rebuilt; the modern city is a different town that took the name.
Yesenin, one of Russia's best-loved poets, was born in a village here.
kaluga: Probably from a word for a bog or a bend in the river.
Tsiolkovsky, the schoolteacher who worked out the mathematics of spaceflight in the 1890s, lived and taught here.
The 1480 stand on the Ugra river in this region ended Mongol overlordship of Russia without a battle being fought.
chelyabinsk: From a Bashkir word, possibly selebe, a hollow or pit.
A meteor exploded over the city in 2013 with the force of 500 kilotons, injuring 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass.
Mayak nearby suffered a nuclear accident in 1957 that was kept secret for thirty years and was among the worst ever.
bashkortostan: "Land of the Bashkirs" — the name may mean "head wolf" or "chief tribe" in Turkic.
It produces almost all of Russia's honey, including wild honey still cut from hollow trees by climbers using ropes.
Shulgan-Tash cave here has painted horses and mammoths about 16,000 years old, the only Palaeolithic cave art in eastern Europe.
tula: Possibly from a word for a hidden or sheltered place.
It has made Russian weapons since 1712 and its samovars since the 1770s — "taking a samovar to Tula" is the Russian coals to Newcastle.
Tolstoy's estate Yasnaya Polyana is here, where he wrote War and Peace and is buried under a mound with no headstone.
chita: The map's older name for Zabaykalsky Krai — "beyond Baikal"; Chita is its capital, from an Evenki word.
The exiled Decembrists were held here after 1826, and their wives followed them into Siberia.
It borders both Mongolia and China, and the Trans-Siberian and the old Chinese Eastern Railway split nearby.
ulyanovsk: Named for Lenin, whose real surname was Ulyanov and who was born here when it was Simbirsk.
Kerensky, the head of the Provisional Government Lenin overthrew, was born in the same town, and his father taught Lenin.
It sits on the Volga, and its bridge is among the longest in Europe at nearly 6 km.
buryat: Named for the Buryats, the largest indigenous people of Siberia, who are Mongolian in language and traditionally Buddhist.
Ivolginsky datsan here is the centre of Russian Buddhism, and holds the body of a lama who died in 1927 and shows little decay.
The republic runs along the eastern shore of Lake Baikal.
khakass: Named for the Khakas people; the name was applied by Soviet ethnographers from a Chinese term for an earlier Yenisei Kyrgyz state.
Its steppe is covered in standing stones and kurgans from the Tagar culture, some 3,000 years old.
The Sayano-Shushenskaya dam here is Russia's largest power station; an accident in 2009 killed 75 people.
samara: From the Samara river, possibly from a Turkic or Iranian word for steppe river.
It was Kuybyshev in Soviet times and was the reserve capital in 1941: a bunker was dug for Stalin 37 m down, and he never used it.
The Zhiguli hills force the Volga into a great loop here, and Soviet rockets including Gagarin's were built in the city.
penza: From the river, probably a Finno-Ugric name.
Meyerhold, the theatre director shot in 1940, was born here, and his house is a museum.
It sits on the forest-steppe border, and its black earth is some of the most fertile in Russia.
amur: Named for the river; the name probably comes from a Tungusic word for water, or from Mongolian amar, meaning rest.
The Vostochny Cosmodrome here is Russia's new spaceport, built to reduce reliance on Baikonur in Kazakhstan.
Its soy fields produce a large share of Russia's crop, and the river is the border with China for 1,700 km.
bryansk: From debryansk, "place of thickets" — debri means dense forest.
Its forests sheltered the largest Soviet partisan movement of the war, tens of thousands of fighters behind German lines.
It was the most heavily contaminated Russian region after Chernobyl, which is over the border in Ukraine.
orel: Russian for "eagle" — legend says one flew up when the founders felled a tree on the site in 1566.
Turgenev was born here and set A Sportsman's Sketches in its countryside.
The battle of Kursk in 1943 was fought partly in this region, in the largest tank engagement in history.
lipetsk: From lipa, the lime tree, which grew along its river.
Peter the Great built ironworks here to arm his new navy, and the town grew around them.
It has one of the largest steel plants in Russia and one of the country's oldest spa waters.
tambov: From a Moksha word, probably tombakov, "abyss" or "deep place".
The Tambov rebellion of 1920–21, a peasant uprising against grain requisitioning, was crushed with poison gas and hostage-taking.
"A Tambov wolf is your comrade" is a Russian phrase for refusing unwanted familiarity.
altay: From a Mongolian or Turkic word, probably altan, "golden" — the golden mountains.
This is the krai, the lowland farming region; the mountainous republic next to it is separate.
It is one of Russia's main grain and buckwheat regions.
orenburg: "Fortress on the Or" — though the town was moved and now sits on the Ural, not the Or.
Its knitted goat-down shawls are so fine that a full-size one passes through a wedding ring.
It was the gateway to Central Asia for the Russian Empire, and the first Soviet space launches were tracked from here.
tuva: Named for the Tuvans, a Turkic people; the republic was an independent state from 1921 to 1944.
Tuvan throat singing, khoomei, produces two or three notes at once and is a UNESCO heritage item.
A monument in Kyzyl marks what Tuvans claim as the geographic centre of Asia.
kursk: From the river Kur, itself probably from a word for a bird or a spring.
The 1943 battle here was the largest tank battle ever fought and ended German offensive capacity in the east.
The Kursk Magnetic Anomaly beneath it is the largest iron ore deposit in the world, and it deflects compass needles.
saratov: Probably from Turkic sary tau, "yellow mountain", for the hills above the Volga.
Gagarin landed in a field in this region in 1961 and was found by a farmer and her granddaughter, who thought he was an alien.
Chernyshevsky, whose novel What Is to Be Done? shaped a generation of revolutionaries, was born here.
gorno-altay: "Mountain Altai" — the republic, as against the lowland krai of the same name.
The Denisovans, a human species known mainly from DNA, were identified from a finger bone found in Denisova cave here.
Its Golden Mountains are a UNESCO site, and the Altai is where four countries and several language families meet.
voronezh: Of uncertain origin — possibly from a personal name or from voron, a raven.
Peter the Great built Russia's first navy here in 1695–96, on a river far from any sea, and sailed it down to the Don.
Its black earth is among the most fertile soil on earth; a cube of it was displayed at the 1900 Paris Exposition as a standard.
belgorod: "White town" — bely white, gorod town, for the chalk hills it stands on.
Those chalk cliffs hold cave monasteries cut by monks, some still in use.
It was the first place to fire a victory salute in the war, in 1943, starting a Soviet tradition.
volgograd: "Volga town" — it was Tsaritsyn, then Stalingrad, then renamed in 1961 during de-Stalinisation.
The battle here in 1942–43 was the bloodiest in history, with perhaps two million casualties, and turned the war.
The Motherland Calls statue on Mamayev Kurgan was the tallest in the world when built, at 85 m with the sword.
sakhalin: From a Manchu name for the Amur, sahaliyan ula, "black river", which mapmakers accidentally attached to the island.
Japan held the southern half from 1905 to 1945, and the Kuril Islands are still disputed between the two countries.
Chekhov travelled here in 1890 to survey the penal colony and wrote a book that shamed the government into reform.
yevrey: The Jewish Autonomous Oblast — yevrey means Jew; it was created in 1934 as a Soviet Jewish homeland in the Far East.
The plan largely failed: Jews never exceeded about a third of the population and are now well under 1%.
Yiddish is still co-official, and the street signs in Birobidzhan are bilingual.
rostov: Rostov-on-Don, named to distinguish it from the older Rostov Veliky near Moscow; the name is from a personal name, Rost.
It is the capital of the Don Cossacks, whose self-governing host held the steppe frontier for the tsars.
Sholokhov's And Quiet Flows the Don, which won the Nobel Prize, is set in its villages.
astrakhan: Probably from Hajji Tarkhan, a title meaning a privileged man who had made the pilgrimage.
It sits on the Volga delta, the largest in Europe, where the river fans into 500 channels before the Caspian.
Most of the world's beluga caviar came from here before the sturgeon collapsed; it is now farmed.
kalmyk: Named for the Kalmyks, who migrated from Dzungaria in the 1600s — the only Buddhist people in Europe.
Stalin deported the entire nation to Siberia in 1943; about half died before they were allowed back in 1957.
Elista, its capital, built a whole district for chess when a chess-obsessed president ran the republic in the 1990s.
primorye: "By the sea" — primorsky, maritime, the standard Russian word for a coastal region.
Vladivostok, "ruler of the east", is the terminus of the Trans-Siberian, 9,289 km from Moscow.
The Amur tiger survives here, about 500 of them, the largest cat in the world.
krasnodar: "Gift of the reds" — renamed in 1920 from Yekaterinodar, "Catherine's gift", for the land she gave the Cossacks.
Sochi in it hosted the 2014 Winter Olympics in a subtropical resort where palms grow.
It is Russia's main agricultural region, growing most of its rice, tea and wine.
stavropol: Greek for "city of the cross", from a cross found when the fortress was built in 1777.
Gorbachev was born and made his career here before Moscow.
Its mineral water spas — Kislovodsk, Pyatigorsk, Yessentuki — have drawn Russians since the 1800s, and Lermontov was killed in a duel at Pyatigorsk.
adygey: Named for the Adyghe, part of the Circassian peoples native to the north-west Caucasus.
Most Circassians were killed or expelled to the Ottoman Empire in the 1860s, and the diaspora today far outnumbers those at home.
Adyghe cheese from here is a protected name, and the republic is an enclave entirely inside Krasnodar Krai.
karachay-cherkess: Two peoples in one name: the Karachay are Turkic, the Cherkess are Circassian, and they speak unrelated languages.
Mount Elbrus stands on its border at 5,642 m, the highest mountain in Europe.
The Arkhyz observatory here has the largest optical telescope in Russia, at 2,070 m.
kabardin-balkar: Again two peoples: the Kabardians are Circassian, the Balkars Turkic, paired by Soviet administrative design.
The Balkars were deported wholesale in 1944 and returned in 1957, like the Kalmyks and Chechens.
Elbrus is shared with the neighbouring republic, and its glaciers feed the rivers of the whole north Caucasus.
chechnya: The Russians named it after a village, Chechen-Aul; the Chechens call themselves Nokhchi and their land Nokhchiyn.
They were deported en masse in 1944 and lost perhaps a quarter of their people; the return began in 1957.
Two wars in the 1990s and 2000s destroyed Grozny almost completely; it has since been rebuilt.
north-ossetia: The Ossetians speak an Iranian language, descended from the Alans and ultimately the Scythians — the only such language in the Caucasus.
South Ossetia across the mountains broke from Georgia, which is why the "north" in the name matters.
The 2004 Beslan school siege here killed 334 people, 186 of them children.
ingush: Named for the Ingush, who call themselves Ghalghai; the Russian name comes from the village of Angusht.
Their medieval stone tower villages in the mountains, built for defence and for the dead, are among the most striking structures in the Caucasus.
They were deported in 1944 alongside the Chechens, with whom they share a closely related language.
dagestan: "Land of mountains" — Turkic dag, mountain, plus Persian stan.
The most linguistically dense place in the world: over thirty languages from three unrelated families in one republic.
Derbent in it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Russia, with a Sasanian wall from the sixth century that is a UNESCO site.
